summary: Discusses common scenarios for connecting an enterprise network to multiple ISPs using provider-assigned address space, and how conditional Router Advertisements could be applied in those scenarios without network prefix translation.

eli5.summary: A company has two internet providers and gives its computers addresses from both. Routers only advertise a provider when it is working.

questions: how do you do enterprise multihoming with ipv6
how to handle multiple isp connections without nat
subtitle: Connecting enterprise networks to multiple ISPs using provider addresses.

tldr.problem: Enterprise networks with multiple ISP connections face a challenge: hosts need addresses from each ISP, but when an ISP connection fails, hosts should stop using that ISP's addresses. Router Advertisements normally cannot communicate this type of dynamic address status.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes conditional Router Advertisements that change the preferred lifetime of address prefixes based on whether the corresponding ISP uplink is operational, encouraging hosts to use different source addresses when links fail.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now implement failover and load-balancing across multiple ISPs without requiring host support for advanced multihoming features, using only standard IPv6 mechanisms.

today: RFC 8475 is an Informational document providing guidance for enterprise networks implementing multihoming with provider-assigned IPv6 addresses. The approach is widely applicable in networks that do not require advanced routing features and provides a practical solution using only standard IPv6 mechanisms.

sections.title: Multihoming Without Translation
sections.content:
Enterprise networks often connect to multiple Internet Service Providers for redundancy and capacity. In IPv4, this typically requires Network Address Translation (NAT) and private addresses because assigning public addresses from multiple providers to the same host creates problems. With IPv6, each ISP assigns a prefix (typically a /48), so hosts can have addresses from multiple providers without translation.

However, this introduces a new problem: when a host has addresses from both ISP_A and ISP_B, it must use only ISP_A's address when sending traffic via ISP_A's link, and ISP_B's address when sending via ISP_B. If ISP_A's link fails, hosts should immediately stop using ISP_A's addresses. The challenge is signaling these changes to hosts dynamically when uplinks go down or come back up.
sections.eli5: With two internet providers, computers need addresses from both. But when one provider's connection breaks, the router needs to tell computers to stop using that provider's addresses right away.

sections.title: Common Multihoming Scenarios
sections.content:
This RFC focuses on two typical enterprise multihoming patterns. In primary/backup mode, one ISP is preferred and all traffic uses its link; the second ISP is only used if the first fails. In load-balancing mode, both ISP links are active simultaneously and traffic is distributed across them, though not necessarily evenly.

The solutions described assume hosts use the default IPv6 address selection algorithm (RFC 6724) and may not support advanced multihoming features like Rule 5.5, which would explicitly prefer source addresses based on the next hop. Enterprise networks often include smartphones and personal devices (BYOD scenarios) that lack these capabilities, so the solution must work without them.
sections.eli5: There are two common ways to use two providers: one as backup (primary/backup) or both at the same time (load-balancing). The solution needs to work with regular computers that do not know about multihoming.

sections.title: The Conditional Router Advertisements Approach
sections.content:
The core idea is to use Router Advertisements (RAs) not just to announce prefixes, but to signal whether hosts should use those prefixes. Every RA includes a preferred_lifetime field for each prefix. When an ISP uplink is operational, the router sends an RA with a nonzero preferred lifetime (for example, 604800 seconds, or one week), which tells hosts that addresses from that prefix are good to use. When the uplink fails, the router sends an RA with preferred_lifetime = 0, which deprecates the prefix—still valid for existing connections, but not preferred for new ones.

The solution also covers DNS: if hosts receive DNS server addresses via Router Advertisement options, those can be similarly deprecated and un-deprecated. The router must remember to maintain these lifetime values in both solicited RAs (when a host asks) and unsolicited periodic RAs, not just send them once during a failure.
sections.eli5: Each internet provider gets an address prefix. When that provider's link works, the router says the addresses are good to use. When it fails, the router says the addresses should not be used for new connections.

sections.title: Configuration Examples
sections.content:
A simple case is a single router with two ISP uplinks. If ISP_A is primary and ISP_B is backup, the router is configured: when ISP_A's uplink is up, advertise ISP_A's prefix as preferred and ISP_B's prefix as deprecated (lifetime 0); when ISP_A fails, swap them. The router also needs a forwarding policy: packets with source addresses from ISP_A must only go to ISP_A, and packets from ISP_B must only go to ISP_B, to avoid anti-spoofing filters.

More complex topologies use two redundant routers with VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol). One router is the VRRP master (active) while the other is backup. The master advertises one ISP's prefix as preferred and the backup advertises the other ISP's prefix as preferred, making source address selection automatic based on which router is active. When an uplink fails, VRRP switches the master role, and RAs automatically change to reflect the new topology.
sections.eli5: In the simplest setup, one router lists which provider is working in its announcements. In a redundant setup, two routers take turns being the main one, and each tells computers about different providers.

sections.title: What the Solution Cannot Do
sections.content:
This approach works only for relatively simple network topologies with straightforward routing. Complex topologies with custom traffic engineering requirements would need more configuration. It also does not preserve TCP connections when an ISP uplink fails—if ISP_A goes down, all active sessions using ISP_A addresses are interrupted because there is no path for return traffic. Recovery of the uplink does not automatically restart those connections.

For load-balancing, the RFC notes that the source address selection algorithm does not consider uplink properties like latency or capacity, so traffic distribution between uplinks may be uneven or suboptimal. Routers should implement damping policies to prevent address flapping if an uplink keeps going down and coming back up rapidly. Additionally, if all uplinks fail simultaneously, all addresses become deprecated, and hosts may fall back to IPv4 or fail-over to private Unique Local Addresses (ULAs).
sections.eli5: This solution only works for simple setups. If a provider goes down, active conversations with that provider will break. The solution does not spread traffic evenly across providers, and if all providers break at once, the computer might switch to IPv4.

sections.title: Security and Protection
sections.content:
Because this solution relies on Router Advertisements, it inherits the same security risks: an attacker who can send rogue RAs can deprecate addresses unexpectedly, force traffic to a backup (possibly more expensive or hostile) ISP, or prevent hosts from reaching the Internet. Network administrators SHOULD secure RAs, typically using RA Guard, a mechanism that filters forged RAs at the network edge.

The RFC notes that no new security vulnerabilities are introduced beyond those already present in standard RA-based address autoconfiguration. Both the mechanism and its limitations are well-understood from years of IPv6 deployment.
sections.eli5: The solution relies on routers telling computers which addresses to use. If a bad actor sends fake announcements, they could trick computers into using the wrong provider. Networks should use RA Guard to block fake announcements.
